As distant Typhoon Dolphin continues west-northwestward, passing 
south of Minamitorishima, the developing monsoon surge near the 
Marianas will shift gradually north, maintaining at least scattered 
showers and isolated thunderstorms in the forecast over the next few 
days. Shower coverage is expected to focus near and south of Guam 
through early next week. Meanwhile, west to southwest winds will 
continue to increase, especially for Guam, then spread northward
across the CNMI. Moderate to fresh winds with occasional strong 
gusts are expected to become breezy Sunday and Sunday night, then 
windy, Monday through Tuesday, with near-gale to gale force gusts 
possible, particularly near any heavier showers. A headline was 
included to highlight the potential for windy conditions to develop 
early next week. Breezy west to southwest winds are expected to 
continue into the end of the week as TY Dolphin continues its west-
northwest track toward the Ryukyu Islands, with sustained wind 
speeds hovering around Small Craft Advisory criteria of 22 knots.

Marine/Surf...
The Gale Watch for Guam coastal waters has been upgraded to a Small 
Craft Advisory. A monsoon pattern, south to southwest of distant 
Typhoon Dolphin will continue to build over the Marianas over the 
coming days. Strong westerlies will develop starting Sunday morning 
across southern Guam coastal waters, generating choppy seas hazardous
to small craft, which will then spread northward across the CNMI 
through early next week. Winds will peak early next week, with a 
possibility of frequent gale-force gusts Monday through Tuesday, 
which would necessitate a Gale Warning at that time. In addition to 
the stronger winds and wind waves, distant Typhoon Dolphin is 
generating a long-period easterly swell that is beginning to move 
through the Marianas, which will gradually shift north early next 
week, then northwest. Meanwhile, the developing monsoon pattern will 
lead to increasing southwesterly swell over the coming days. These 
increasing swells and wind waves will build combined seas to exceed 
10 feet across the coastal waters, maintaining hazardous sea 
conditions for much of the coming week.

Currently, there is a moderate risk of rip currents along east, 
west, north, and south facing reefs. Long-period east to northeast 
swell, emanating from distant Typhoon Dolphin, is expected to develop
a high risk of rip currents along east-facing reefs of the Marianas 
beginning Sunday afternoon, and a High Rip Current Risk has been
issued. As Dolphin passes the far northern CNMI, the long-period 
swell direction is expected to shift north early next week, and then 
northwest. As it does so, a high risk of rip currents, and hazardous 
surf, is expected to develop along north, then west facing reefs next
week. There will be a moderate risk of lightning through at least 
Sunday night.

Tropical Systems...
Typhoon Dolphin has weakened slightly, down to sustained winds of 
140 mph. It continues to slowly move away from Wake Island, south of 
Minamitorishima, and slowly towards Iwo To. Although Dolphin may 
briefly strengthen slightly tonight, a gradual weakening trend is 
expected for Monday through Wednesday. However, mariners 
transitioning between Iwo To and the Marianas or Micronesia need to 
continue monitoring Dolphin's progress, as it's forecast to still be 
a typhoon as it passes by Iwo To. As such, significant swell will 
still impact mariners traversing these areas. Additionally, a 
burgeoning wind field associated with the monsoon trough will lift 
north across the Marianas, bringing squall-like conditions as the 
region is enveloped in the monsoon trough. This will be accompanied 
by periodic reductions in visibility along with increased 
thunderstorm potential.

For more information on Dolphin, please refer to either the Tropical
Cyclone Warning, WTPN31 PGTW from the Joint Typhoon Warning Center,
or the Tropical Cyclone Public Advisory, WTPQ31 PGUM from the
National Weather Service.

Eastern Micronesia...
The main focus was centered on winds and swell, as late even
scatterometer data from yesterday combined with the midnight data 
run showed a burgeoning wind field northwest and north of Pohnpei.
CDIP data from the Marshall islands also showed a northwest swell.
With this in mind, focus was placed on the short term (next 48 hours)
of wind and swell heights at Pohnpei and Kosrae, as you're still
seeing the "side effects" of Typhoon Dolphin. As such, wind waves 
were maintained above the "conventional one foot per 5 knots" 
concept, while "graduating" the swell directions as the cross- 
equatorial swell "meshes" (mixes) with the distant Dolphin 
northwesterly swell. Additionally, you're still seeing some of the
